<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README provided, the project is an open-source, modular JavaScript/TypeScript library for measuring real-user performance metrics – specifically the Web Vitals. It is designed to be embedded in web pages to report metrics such as CLS, FCP, FID (deprecated), INP, LCP, and TTFB. The library also supports two “builds” (standard and attribution) and provides integrations for analytics systems like Google Analytics and Tag Manager.

Below is a step‐by‐step explanation of how to create a detailed system design/architecture diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the main components:
   • Library API / Entry Points: At the highest level, the API functions (such as onCLS, onFCP, onLCP, onINP, onTTFB, and the deprecated onFID) act as the main interface to the library.
   • Core Measurement Modules: In the “src” directory you have modules dedicated to each metric (for example, files under src/attribution for the attribution build and the separate metric files like onCLS.ts, onFCP.ts, etc.). 
   • Utility and Helper Modules: The “src/lib” folder contains utility functions (e.g., getUniqueID, doubleRAF, observe functions, polyfill implementations) that support the core metric calculations and event handling.
   • Type Definitions: The “src/types” folder provides TypeScript type definitions (e.g., for defining Metric interfaces such as CLSMetric, FCPMetric, etc.) that ensure type safety and consistency.
   • Build & Bundling Infrastructure: Files such as rollup.config.js and package.json indicate a modern build process where the code is bundled into different formats (ES module, UMD, IIFE) for different usage scenarios. 
   • Testing Infrastructure: The “test” directory (with subdirectories for unit tests, end-to-end tests, and integration tests) is used to verify the functionality of the library across different browsers and conditions.
   • Documentation & Contribution Guides: The docs and markdown files (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, etc.) explain usage, integrations, and developer guidelines.

2. Detail the relationships and interactions:
   • The API Methods (e.g., onCLS, onLCP) act as the entry points for developers’ code. These functions use the Performance Observer API and other browser performance APIs under the hood.
   • Each API method calls helper/util modules from the “src/lib” folder to handle low-level tasks (e.g., scheduling functions with doubleRAF, binding reporters, observing performance events).
   • The computed metric objects are created and structured using types defined in “src/types” and potentially augmented with additional debugging data when using the attribution build (from files in src/attribution).
   • From a build perspective, these source files are transpiled and bundled (using Rollup, as set up by rollup.config.js) into various module formats which are then published as npm packages and/or used as CDN-hosted scripts.

3. Highlight the architectural patterns and design principles:
   • Modularity and Separation of Concerns: Each metric function is isolated in its own module, and utility functions are decoupled from main functionality, making maintenance and future extensions easier.
   • Dual Build Strategy: There are two distinct “builds” – the standard one and an attribution-enhanced variant. This abstraction allows developers to choose between minimal payloads and a more detailed debugging version.
   • Event-driven Architecture: The library reacts to performance events (exposed via PerformanceObserver), and these events uniquely drive the measurement reporting.
   • Safe use of Browser APIs: The design relies on modern browser APIs and gracefully handles scenarios where an API may not support certain metrics (e.g., falling back when the navigation entry isn’t available).

4. Provide guidelines on visualizing technology and flows in the diagram:
   • Start with a high-level “client browser” box. Within it, show the Performance API (like PerformanceObserver, Navigation Timing, etc.) that are directly tapped into by the library.
   • Inside the browser, depict the “Web Vitals Library” block. Within this block, subdivide it further into three layers:
       - API Layer: Represents the functions that external code calls (onCLS, onLCP, onINP, etc.).
       - Measurement/Processing Layer: Contains the individual modules (files under src/attribution and the separate metric files) connected to utility modules in src/lib. Draw arrows from the API functions to the utility functions and from there to the underlying browser APIs.
       - Data Typing and Structuring: Denote the “types” component that standardizes the metric objects.
   • Include an “Integration / Reporting” external component representing analytics endpoints (Google Analytics, Tag Manager, custom endpoints) with arrows flowing from the API layer (or reporting modules) toward these external systems.
   • Draw a separate box for “Build Infrastructure” (Rollup, TypeScript) that transforms the “src” code into the distributed builds. Show arrows from “src” to “dist” demonstrating the build process.
   • Mark separate test modules (unit tests, end-to-end tests) in another box that interacts with the main library modules to ensure behavior under various scenarios.
   • Use clear labels on each component (e.g., “API Entry Points”, “Utility Functions”, “Type Definitions”, “Attribution Modules”, “Build & Bundling”, “Test Suite”) with directional arrows annotating data flow.

5. Design styling details:
   • Use distinct shapes (e.g., rectangles for modules, cylinders for databases/integrations if needed, or parallelograms for processing modules) and consistent color coding (for example, one color for public APIs, a different color for internal utilities, and yet another for external integrations).
   • Include directional arrows that indicate the flow of data: for instance, show how performance events flow from the Performance Observer API to the measurement functions, and then how these metrics are passed on to the reporting functions.
   • Clearly label edges with brief notes, such as “measures layout shift”, “reports metric via callback”, “build process transpires with Rollup”, etc.

6. Tailor instructions to an open-source library:
   • Emphasize that the diagram should clearly separate concerns within the library: the measurement logic (handling browser APIs and events), the API exposure (functions like onCLS, onLCP, etc.), and the build process that converts the modular source code (from TypeScript) into distributable bundles.
   • Note that while it isn’t a full-stack application, there are external dependencies (analytics endpoints, browser APIs) that must be represented.
   • Since the library supports two builds (standard versus attribution), explicitly show the branching in the abstraction – one path including additional attribution data before the metric is reported.

In summary, instruct the principal software engineer to design the diagram with:
   • A clear division between external browser APIs, internal measurement modules (divided into API, processing, and type-definition layers), and external integrations.
   • Directional arrows showing the flow from raw performance data (observed events) through processing to output (reporting/debugging), as well as the build process converting source modules into consumable formats.
   • Annotations for key architectural patterns like modulated design, event-driven processing, and the dual build strategy.

This detailed diagram will effectively capture all essential architectural elements and interactions specific to the web-vitals library, making it easy for future maintainers and integrators to understand and work with the code base.
</explanation>
